articles.title: Rochdale Cultural Organisations to Receive Share of £15 Million Funding
articles.excerpt: Cultural organisations in Rochdale will benefit from a £15 million funding package aimed at enhancing community engagement and wellbeing across Greater Manchester over the next three years.
articles.content_html:
Cultural organisations in Rochdale are set to benefit from a £15 million funding package announced by the Greater Manchester Combined Authority (GMCA). This investment aims to enhance the impact of cultural initiatives on local communities and is part of Mayor Bev Craig's commitment to revitalise community pride and provide engaging activities across the region.

The funding will be distributed over three years and will support various organisations, including grassroots music venues, community theatres, and local production companies. The initiative focuses on promoting wellbeing, community cohesion, and growth through cultural participation, youth engagement, and disability arts.

Among the recipients is Breaking Barriers, a Rochdale-based multidisciplinary production company that collaborates with local communities to amplify unheard voices. The company has been awarded £40,000 annually from the GMCA Culture Fund for the years 2026 to 2029. Parvez Qadir, the Artistic Director of Breaking Barriers, expressed excitement about the funding, highlighting its significance in supporting communities and fostering cultural interventions.

This funding represents a significant opportunity for local cultural organisations to expand their reach and impact, ultimately contributing to a more vibrant community life in Rochdale. Further details on specific projects and initiatives funded by this package are expected to be released in the coming months.

Rochdale will welcome a new live music initiative this Friday, September 22, with the launch of the Early Doors Club at St Chad's Church. This series aims to offer high-quality performances without the burden of expensive tickets or late nights, allowing attendees to enjoy music in a community setting.

The Early Doors Club, which began in Wigan, focuses on hosting concerts in unconventional venues such as cafes, churches, and social clubs. The concept is designed to make live music accessible, with events starting early in the evening, allowing guests to return home by 9 PM. Attendees are encouraged to pay what they can afford for entry.

The inaugural concert at St Chad's Church will feature Liam Fender, a singer-songwriter known for his depth and honesty. He is also the brother of popular artist Sam Fender, although he has established his own identity in the music scene. The Early Doors Club expressed excitement about welcoming Fender back for this special event.

This new venue is expected to enrich the local cultural landscape, providing residents with an opportunity to experience live music in a familiar and welcoming environment. The Early Doors Club aims to continue its mission of making live music accessible to all, and this launch marks an important step in that direction.

articles.title: Inquest Finds Drink-Driving Contributed to Heywood Man's Fatal Crash
articles.excerpt: An inquest jury has cleared Greater Manchester Police of any wrongdoing following a high-speed chase that resulted in the death of 23-year-old Will Place in Rochdale on July 1, 2024.
articles.content_html:
BREAKING NEWS — LIVE

Live updates, newest first.

02:03, 23 September 2026

An inquest jury has concluded that Will Place, 23, died after drink-driving at excessive speeds before crashing into a pub in Heywood.

An inquest jury has cleared Greater Manchester Police of any wrongdoing following a high-speed chase that resulted in the death of 23-year-old Will Place after crashing into a pub in Heywood.

An inquest jury has cleared Greater Manchester Police of any wrongdoing following a high-speed chase that resulted in the death of 23-year-old Will Place in Rochdale on July 1, 2024.

23:48, 22 September 2026

An inquest has determined that Will Place, 23, died after crashing his car into a pub in Heywood while over the drink-drive limit following a football match.

23:21, 22 September 2026

An inquest jury has concluded that Will Place, 23, died after drink-driving at excessive speeds before crashing into a pub in Heywood, following a night of drinking after an England football match.

23:09, 22 September 2026

An inquest jury has concluded that Will Place, 23, died after drink-driving at excessive speeds before crashing into the White Lion pub in Heywood.

21:30, 22 September 2026

An inquest jury has cleared Greater Manchester Police of any wrongdoing in the fatal crash of 23-year-old Will Place, which occurred during a high-speed pursuit in Rochdale on July 1, 2024.

An inquest jury has determined that Greater Manchester Police officers acted appropriately during a high-speed pursuit that ended in the fatal crash of 23-year-old Will Place in Rochdale on July 1, 2024. The incident occurred after Place, who had been drinking, ran a red light in front of a marked police van, prompting officers to initiate a chase.

The pursuit began at approximately 3:00 a.m. after Place left a local venue where he had watched an England soccer match. Officers reported that the vehicle reached speeds of up to 70 mph in 30 mph zones. However, police control instructed officers to discontinue the chase shortly after it began due to a lack of tactical pursuit resources. Despite this, Place lost control of his vehicle and crashed into the White Lion pub at the junction of Rochdale Road and York Street, resulting in a fire and partial building collapse.

During the inquest at Rochdale Coroner's Court, PC Sarah Hardman, who was driving the pursuing police van, explained that she activated her emergency lights and sirens after witnessing Place's reckless driving. She stated that the decision to pursue was proportionate at the time, and she believed it was her duty to attempt to stop the vehicle to prevent further danger. The chase was called off before the crash occurred, and she did not activate her body-worn camera as her focus was on driving safely.

The inquest also revealed that toxicology tests indicated Place's blood alcohol level was 163mg per decilitre, which is more than double the legal limit. Family members expressed their grief over his loss, with his mother, Beverley Place, describing him as a loving and thoughtful young man who had a promising future ahead of him.

articles.title: Rochdale Residents Invited to Join Great British Dog Walk for Hearing Dogs Charity
articles.excerpt: The Great British Dog Walk encourages locals to explore Rochdale’s scenic routes while raising funds for Hearing Dogs for Deaf People, with a target of 70 miles throughout October.
articles.content_html:
Residents of Rochdale are encouraged to lace up their walking boots this October for the Great British Dog Walk, an initiative by the charity Hearing Dogs for Deaf People. Participants are invited to walk a total of 70 miles throughout the month, exploring the town’s scenic trails and historic landmarks while raising vital funds to support the training of hearing dogs for deaf individuals.

The 70-mile target represents the average lifetime cost of £70,000 to train and support a single hearing dog. By turning everyday walks into sponsored miles, participants will help fund the breeding, socialisation, and specialised training required to match these dogs with those who need them most.

The campaign is open to walkers of all ages and abilities, encouraging the community to discover new routes or enhance their regular walking paths. The initiative is supported by a local puppy training hub, which plays a crucial role in the charity's mission to transform the lives of deaf people across the region.

As the month progresses, participants can track their mileage and share their experiences, contributing to a collective effort that not only promotes physical activity but also raises awareness about the importance of hearing dogs. For more information on how to get involved, residents can visit the Hearing Dogs for Deaf People website.

articles.title: Why does Rochdale say ‘cruckle’?
articles.excerpt: A short look at a small local verb: what ‘cruckle’ means in Rochdale, where it comes from and why linguists find it interesting.
articles.summary: A short look at a small local verb: what ‘cruckle’ means in Rochdale, where it comes from and why linguists find it interesting.
articles.body:
Anyone who grew up in parts of Rochdale will recognise the complaint: “I cruckled my ankle.” Locally, to “cruckle” (also heard as “cruckled”) is used to mean rolling or twisting one’s ankle — the awkward half‑stumble you can often walk off but which still makes you wince. This sense turns up repeatedly in folk descriptions of Rochdale speech and in the Manchester area project work that asked residents to name words they associate with each borough. ([cambridge.org](https://www.cambridge.org/core/services/aop-cambridge-core/content/view/252F7E107074D13952BD49873C6F53B8/S2049754724000106a.pdf/broad_strong_and_soft_using_geospatial_analysis_to_understand_folklinguistic_terminology.pdf))

The word’s association with Rochdale is not just anecdote. A 2024 perceptual‑dialectology study of Greater Manchester (the “draw‑a‑map / keywords” method) collected 349 participants’ comments about local accents and vocabulary; in the dataset “cruckle” (spelt there as “cruckle”/“cruckled”) appears among words respondents list for Rochdale alongside other locally salient items such as “guinnel” (ginnel). That academic study — published in the Journal of Linguistic Geography — presents the word as part of residents’ folk‑linguistic map of the borough. ([cambridge.org](https://www.cambridge.org/core/services/aop-cambridge-core/content/view/252F7E107074D13952BD49873C6F53B8/S2049754724000106a.pdf/broad_strong_and_soft_using_geospatial_analysis_to_understand_folklinguistic_terminology.pdf))

But ‘cruckle’ is not an accidental modern invention. Historical dialect lexicography records older relatives of the form — crookle, crunkle, crankle and similar spellings — with meanings in the same semantic field: to bend, make crooked, crumple, stoop or hobble. Joseph Wright’s English Dialect Dictionary (late 19th century) records crookle in northern and midland counties with senses that fit those older meanings; other historical glossaries and etymological work link crook‑/crunk‑ roots to words for bending and rumpling. In Scots dialect lexicons the cognate crunkle has long been attested with senses like “to crumple” or “to make a rustling/crackling sound.” These sources show that the form family is old and regional rather than a brand‑new local coinage. ([archive.org](https://archive.org/details/englishdialectdi01wrig))

So why does Rochdale use it to mean twisting an ankle? Part of the answer is semantic extension and local persistence. Roots meaning “bend” or “crumple” naturally extend to bodily movement — stooping, limping, or twisting a limb — and the frequentative/agentive endings that appear in dialect verbs (‑le, ‑le‑type forms) are common in northern English and Scots. Over generations a local pronunciation and narrow semantic focus (here, an ankle‑roll) can become the everyday sense people use and recognise. Linguists therefore see Rochdale’s “cruckle” as a local survival and narrowing of a wider, older dialect verb group rather than a wholly unique word created in isolation. ([archive.org](https://archive.org/details/englishdialectdi01wrig))

Is ‘cruckle’ unique to Rochdale? That depends on how you count uniqueness. Perceptual and folk‑linguistic evidence show Rochdale residents and many Greater Manchester respondents strongly associate the word with the borough; that social recognition is an important part of the word’s identity. At the same time, historical records show related forms elsewhere in northern England and in Scots: dialect words seldom obey modern administrative borders. In short, the root is regional but the living habit and local pride in “I cruckled” feel especially Rochdale. ([cambridge.org](https://www.cambridge.org/core/services/aop-cambridge-core/content/view/252F7E107074D13952BD49873C6F53B8/S2049754724000106a.pdf/broad_strong_and_soft_using_geospatial_analysis_to_understand_folklinguistic_terminology.pdf))

Why do dialect researchers pay attention to small words like this? Because they do two jobs at once: they reveal how people actually speak now and they show how non‑linguists think about place and identity. Words such as “cruckle” become data points for change, contact (for example Lancashire–Yorkshire effects across town boundaries), and social meaning — little markers people use to signal where they are from. Projects that combine historical dictionaries with contemporary perceptual mapping give a fuller picture: an old verb family survives in a recognisably local form, and that form is part of how Rochdalians hear and describe themselves. ([cambridge.org](https://www.cambridge.org/core/services/aop-cambridge-core/content/view/252F7E107074D13952BD49873C6F53B8/S2049754724000106a.pdf/broad_strong_and_soft_using_geospatial_analysis_to_understand_folklinguistic_terminology.pdf))

If you don’t know the word, try it next time you take a tumble in a ginnel — you’ll likely get a nod of recognition from someone from round here. If you want to follow up, the perceptual study (Dann et al., Journal of Linguistic Geography, 2024) and the older dialect dictionaries are good starting points: one gives contemporary social mapping, the others give the historical spread and senses that help explain how the Rochdale meaning developed. ([cambridge.org](https://www.cambridge.org/core/services/aop-cambridge-core/content/view/252F7E107074D13952BD49873C6F53B8/S2049754724000106a.pdf/broad_strong_and_soft_using_geospatial_analysis_to_understand_folklinguistic_terminology.pdf))

Historical dialect lexicography records older relatives of the form — crookle, crunkle, crankle and similar spellings — with meanings in the same semantic field: to bend, make crooked, crumple, stoop or hobble. Joseph Wright’s English Dialect Dictionary (late 19th century) records crookle in northern and midland counties with senses that fit those older meanings; other historical glossaries and etymological work link crook‑/crunk‑ roots to words for bending and rumpling. In Scots dialect lexicons the cognate crunkle has long been attested with senses like “to crumple” or “to make a rustling/crackling sound.” These sources show that the form family is old and regional rather than a brand‑new local coinage. ([archive.org](https://archive.org/details/englishdialectdi01wrig))

So why does Rochdale use it to mean twisting an ankle? Part of the answer is semantic extension and local persistence. Roots meaning “bend” or “crumple” naturally extend to bodily movement — stooping, limping, or twisting a limb — and the frequentative/agentive endings that appear in dialect verbs (‑le, ‑le‑type forms) are common in northern English and Scots. Over generations a local pronunciation and narrow semantic focus (here, an ankle‑roll) can become the everyday sense people use and recognise. Linguists therefore see Rochdale’s “cruckle” as a local survival and narrowing of a wider, older dialect verb group rather than a wholly unique word created in isolation. ([archive.org](https://archive.org/details/englishdialectdi01wrig))

Is ‘cruckle’ unique to Rochdale? That depends on how you count uniqueness. Perceptual and folk‑linguistic evidence show Rochdale residents and many Greater Manchester respondents strongly associate the word with the borough; that social recognition is an important part of the word’s identity. At the same time, historical records show related forms elsewhere in northern England and in Scots: dialect words seldom obey modern administrative borders. In short, the root is regional but the living habit and local pride in “I cruckled” feel especially Rochdale. ([cambridge.org](https://www.cambridge.org/core/services/aop-cambridge-core/content/view/252F7E107074D13952BD49873C6F53B8/S2049754724000106a.pdf/broad_strong_and_soft_using_geospatial_analysis_to_understand_folklinguistic_terminology.pdf))

Why do dialect researchers pay attention to small words like this? Because they do two jobs at once: they reveal how people actually speak now and they show how non‑linguists think about place and identity. Words such as “cruckle” become data points for change, contact (for example Lancashire–Yorkshire effects across town boundaries), and social meaning — little markers people use to signal where they are from. Projects that combine historical dictionaries with contemporary perceptual mapping give a fuller picture: an old verb family survives in a recognisably local form, and that form is part of how Rochdalians hear and describe themselves. ([cambridge.org](https://www.cambridge.org/core/services/aop-cambridge-core/content/view/252F7E107074D13952BD49873C6F53B8/S2049754724000106a.pdf/broad_strong_and_soft_using_geospatial_analysis_to_understand_folklinguistic_terminology.pdf))

If you don’t know the word, try it next time you take a tumble in a ginnel — you’ll likely get a nod of recognition from someone from round here. If you want to follow up, the perceptual study (Dann et al., Journal of Linguistic Geography, 2024) and the older dialect dictionaries are good starting points: one gives contemporary social mapping, the others give the historical spread and senses that help explain how the Rochdale meaning developed. ([cambridge.org](https://www.cambridge.org/core/services/aop-cambridge-core/content/view/252F7E107074D13952BD49873C6F53B8/S2049754724000106a.pdf/broad_strong_and_soft_using_geospatial_analysis_to_understand_folklinguistic_terminology.pdf))

articles.title: Hopwood Hall College Unveils Ambitious Five-Year Vision at Rochdale Town Hall
articles.excerpt: During a recent event at Rochdale Town Hall, Hopwood Hall College launched a new five-year strategy aimed at driving growth and creating opportunities across the borough and beyond.
articles.content_html:
Hopwood Hall College has unveiled an ambitious new strategy for the future during an event held at Rochdale Town Hall. Principal and CEO Julia Heap OBE presented a bold five-year vision designed to drive growth, transform lives, and create new opportunities across the borough and beyond.

The launch event brought together students, staff, and local stakeholders to discuss the college's plans, which aim to enhance educational offerings and support community development. Heap emphasised the importance of collaboration with local businesses and organisations to ensure that the college meets the evolving needs of the community.

This new strategy is expected to focus on expanding vocational training and improving student support services, which will help prepare students for the workforce and further education.

As the college embarks on this new era, it is likely to engage with local residents and businesses to gather feedback and support for its initiatives.

articles.title: Final Opportunity to View Hidden Documents and Artefacts in Rochdale
articles.excerpt: Rochdale's Local Studies Centre and Square Gallery are showcasing previously unseen documents and artefacts until the end of September, highlighting the town's rich heritage.
articles.content_html:
Time is running out for residents to view a unique collection of documents and artefacts that have been hidden in Rochdale's archives. The display, which is part of the Unlocking Collections project, is currently available for viewing at the Rochdale Local Studies Centre and the Square Gallery on Rochdale Town Hall Square until the end of September.

The project, a collaboration between Rochdale Local Studies and the Co-operative Heritage Trust, involved ten volunteers who meticulously searched through various documents, donations, and purchases that reflect the town's heritage. Their efforts have culminated in an exhibition that brings local stories to life through artwork inspired by the archives.

Rochdale Local Studies Centre shared on social media, thanking the volunteers for their creativity and hard work. The exhibition showcases the innovative and radical history of Rochdale, with documents that have accumulated over time through generous contributions from the community.

Residents and visitors are encouraged to take advantage of this final opportunity to explore the rich history of Rochdale before the exhibition concludes. For more information, visit the Rochdale Local Studies Centre or the Square Gallery.

articles.title: Are there really fairies in Healey Dell?
articles.excerpt: The rocky cleft known locally as the Fairies’ Chapel is a real landscape feature with a long history of storytelling — but the supernatural claims sit in folklore, not the council’s records.
articles.summary: The rocky cleft known locally as the Fairies’ Chapel is a real landscape feature with a long history of storytelling — but the supernatural claims sit in folklore, not the council’s records.
articles.body:
Healey Dell’s Fairies’ Chapel is one of those place‑names that makes you stop on the riverside path and look twice. Tucked under the dramatic Victorian viaduct where the River Spodden squeezes through a narrow gorge known locally as “the Thrutch”, a small waterfall and water‑worn cavity in the rock have been likened by generations of visitors to a pulpit, seats and an alcove — and that resemblance is the simple, documented reason for the name.

What is documented

Healey Dell is managed and promoted as a nature reserve by Rochdale Borough Council and is an established local attraction for walkers, schools and families. The borough’s public information describes the site as a beauty spot rich in industrial archaeology — mills, lodges, waterways and the disused Lancashire & Yorkshire Railway viaduct that towers over the Dell. The viaduct itself is recorded on the National Heritage List for England (listed Grade II), confirming the area’s clear industrial and built‑heritage significance. Local guides and the Healey Dell Heritage Centre also record that the river carved a hollow in the rock that early visitors described as church‑like; those water‑worn shapes are a natural feature, the product of erosion over long periods and of particular flood events that changed the valley’s appearance. The Heritage Centre’s own guides and trail maps point to the Fairies’ Chapel as a named point of interest in the reserve and explain the site’s mix of nature, industrial remains and local story‑telling.

One important, verifiable event helps explain why the Chapel looks different now from how 19th‑century writers described it: an extreme storm on 4 July 1838 (commonly called the July Flood) caused severe flooding through the Spodden valley, washed away bridges and damaged mills — contemporary and later local records note that parts of the rock cavity known as the Fairies’ Chapel were altered or destroyed by that event. That is a documented landscape change, not a tale.

What the stories say

The supernatural side of Healey Dell belongs to folklore. Local and Victorian‑era accounts collected in guidebooks, verse and oral tradition mix fairy lore, a so‑called Fairy Queen, tales of witches turned to stone and even a loose connection to regional Robin Hood‑type stories in popular retellings. These stories treat the rock cavity as a “chapel” for the fair folk and describe meetings, prophecies and magical happenings. Local interpretation and visitor materials at the Heritage Centre celebrate these traditions as part of Healey Dell’s cultural heritage.

What we can — and cannot — verify

We can verify the place‑name, the nature‑reserve status, the existence of the viaduct and the effects of the 1838 flood from council records and heritage listings. We can also verify that Victorian and later local guides recorded fairy legends associated with the site and that the Heritage Centre re‑publishes these tales as part of its local‑history interpretation.

What we cannot verify are claims of actual supernatural events. There are no official records, inspections or historical documents that prove the existence of fairies, a Fairy King, or witches being turned to stone in Healey Dell. Those elements belong to oral tradition, local verse and the imaginative accounts that have grown up around the striking rock shapes. When guides or storytellers link Healey Dell to prophetic fairy queens or dramatic magical episodes, they are recounting folklore rather than reporting a verifiable historical event.

Why the mix matters

Places like Healey Dell matter precisely because they gather both stones and stories. The geology and industrial archaeology give the Dell its real, provable history; the fairy tales give it local colour and a living tradition that attracts visitors and sparks imagination — including events, trail materials and seasonal storytelling organised by the Heritage Centre. For readers: you can enjoy the Fairies’ Chapel as a quiet, atmospheric spot shaped by water and time, and as a place where Rochdale’s folklore is still remembered. But if you want official facts about land management, listed structures, or landscape change, those belong to council and heritage records; the fairies remain, for now, in the stories.

articles.title: Liverpool U21s Draw 3-3 with Rochdale Before Losing on Penalties in Jersey Mike's Trophy
articles.excerpt: Rochdale AFC faced Liverpool U21 in a thrilling EFL Trophy match on September 22, 2026, ending in a dramatic 3-3 draw, with Liverpool winning 7-6 on penalties.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale AFC played to a dramatic 3-3 draw against Liverpool Under-21s in the EFL Trophy at the Crown Oil Arena on September 22, 2026. The match, which was part of the Northern Group H fixture, saw both teams showcase their resilience and attacking prowess, ultimately leading to a penalty shootout where Liverpool triumphed 7-6.

The game began with Rochdale taking the lead through Devante Rodney, who scored from distance after Liverpool's Mor Talla Ndiaye was sent off for denying a clear goalscoring opportunity. Liverpool equalised just before half-time with a solo effort from Will Wright, but Rochdale responded with two goals from veteran Ian Henderson, who scored a remarkable chip shot from outside the area, putting his team ahead 3-1.

Liverpool, despite being a man down, fought back with substitutes Ben Trueman and Josh Sonni-Lambie scoring in quick succession to level the match at 3-3, sending the game to penalties after a tense second half. The penalty shootout saw both teams exchange goals, but ultimately Liverpool's goalkeeper Harvey Davies made a crucial save against Sam Waller, allowing Daniel Onanuga to convert the decisive penalty for the young Reds.

This result leaves both Rochdale and Liverpool U21 with one point in the group as they aim for progression in the EFL Trophy. The match was officiated by referee Gareth Sheffield, who has previously overseen matches at Spotland.
